exhibit.headline: Page Nine
exhibit.dek: A $1.5 million in-car video purchase. A separate plate-reader contract signed four months earlier. A two-page form that says a component was “mistakenly left off.” And, three years later, a City platform configured to share plate detections with at least 155 government agencies — none of which the records can date.

standing.grammar_note: Three things are kept apart everywhere in this exhibit: what a document says, which layer of the record it comes from, and which procurement chain or time plane it belongs to.
standing.config_not_use: Configured to share. Not shown to have shared.
standing.config_not_use_long: Every relationship shown from the August 2026 export is a setting in the City’s own platform. No transfer, query, hit or viewing record exists in anything produced.
standing.no_dates: The records reviewed do not establish when any sharing relationship was configured.
standing.clerk_file_caveat: The 25-page file is the City Clerk’s roll-call file as produced in August 2026. Whether these pages were before council members on 20 November 2023 is not established.
standing.no_intent: This exhibit reports structure, not motive. Nothing in it establishes concealment, intent or misconduct by anyone, that any description was false, or that anyone was given a wrong impression.
standing.legend_line: Open rings and dashed connectors show settings in the City’s own platform export. They do not show that any plate record was sent or viewed.

chapters.heading: A $1.5 million in-car video purchase
chapters.body: On 20 November 2023 the Des Moines City Council approved the purchase of M500 in-car video systems and Video Manager from Motorola Solutions, Inc. for $1,500,080, under a Sourcewell cooperative contract, and authorised the Mayor to execute a short form agreement and addendum already on file with the City Clerk.
chapters.consequence: It was agenda item 32, adopted inside a consent agenda covering items 3 through 38 on a single roll call.

chapters.heading: What the council-facing summary described
chapters.body: The supporting council communication described the purchase as “upgraded in-car video systems with installation, implementation, and video evidence management software.” Its synopsis describes replacing cameras and integrating body-worn video. It is accurate as far as it goes.
chapters.consequence: Across the resolution and the council communication — pages 1 to 4 — there is no occurrence of ALPR, LPR, license plate, Vigilant, LEARN, PlateSearch, VehicleManager, hot list, retention or data sharing.

chapters.heading: Twenty-five pages in the clerk’s file
chapters.body: Behind those four pages sit twenty-one more: the short form agreement, then three addenda, then an amendment. The file contains no quote, no line items and no pricing breakdown below the total.
chapters.consequence: Move through it. The four council-facing pages are one layer. The attachments are another.

chapters.heading: The sharing clause, where it appears
chapters.body: On page 9 of the 25-page file, the Mobile Video Addendum reaches §4.5. Plate-recognition data collected by the City is the City’s data, subject to the City’s own retention policy — and the City “at its option, may share its LPR data with other similarly situated Law Enforcement Agencies … by selecting this option within Vigilant VehicleManager.”
chapters.consequence: Sharing with another qualifying agency requires nothing but a setting. The agreement requires no memorandum, no notice, no review and no approval.

chapters.heading: The plate-reader lines were priced elsewhere
chapters.body: The ordering document behind the purchase — a quote dated 23 October 2023 — prices 130 plate-reader licences at $516 each, $67,080, plus a $500 support line. $67,580 of plate-reader licensing inside a $1,500,080 purchase. That quote is not in the 25-page file.
chapters.consequence: And the licence layer is not the deployment: the delivery pack list records a component the vendor calls an “M500 ALPR DVR” on every one of the 130 systems.

chapters.heading: A second procurement, signed earlier
chapters.body: Four months before the council vote, the City contracted separately for the plate-reader platform itself. A different vendor — Vigilant Solutions, LLC. A different cooperative — the Houston-Galveston Area Council. A different city agreement — W23-383, with a term beginning 1 July 2023. Under it: the hosted LEARN account, three years of commercially acquired national vehicle-location data for $33,750, and fixed roadside cameras for $56,770.
chapters.consequence: Every one of those instruments was executed between 1 July and 29 September 2023, by administrative signature. No council action for any of them appears in the records reviewed. Not a Flock system: the cooperative vehicles here are Sourcewell and H-GAC.

chapters.heading: “Mistakenly left off”
chapters.body: The council resolution recites that the systems “have been competitively bid.” The solicitation behind that cooperative contract — issued in November 2019 for public-safety video surveillance — contains no reference to license plates at all. Plate readers were added to the price list on 14 September 2021, by a two-page vendor change request.
chapters.consequence: Its justification field reads: “WatchGuard Video mistakenly left off a key component of our VaaS offering – The License Plate Reader (LPR). It is now included in the VaaS price list.” Five change forms for that contract were identified in 2021. The change-request mechanism is expressly authorised by the contract; whether any scope determination was made is not found in the records produced.

chapters.heading: 2023 record → 2026 configuration snapshot
chapters.body: Everything above is dated. Everything below is a snapshot taken on one morning in August 2026.
chapters.consequence: The records reviewed do not establish when each sharing relationship was configured. Nothing below can be connected in time to anything above.

chapters.heading: At least 155 configured sharing relationships
chapters.body: On 17 August 2026 the City generated three reports from its VehicleManager account. The sharing report, filtered to “Data type : Detection, Sharing status : Sharing,” lists 155 agencies in 36 states and the District of Columbia. 141 are outside Iowa. Five rows are typed Federal. The inbound side shows 120 receiving, 15 with no receiving relationship, 12 approval required and 8 declined.
chapters.consequence: 151 of the 155 rows carry no usable date. Because the export is filtered, 155 is a floor, not a ceiling. Configured to share. Not shown to have shared.

chapters.heading: What the record cannot show
chapters.body: Four different things must be held apart. What the City retains. What the City produced. What the contract allows. And what any actual transfer is established to show.
chapters.consequence: The City stated that search logs “are not something the City generates or keeps copies of.” Department policy nonetheless requires regular audits of ALPR inquiries, and one audit entry in the record reviewed 500 records. The only audit right in the agreement runs from the vendor to the City. No City-side audit, inspection or log-access right appears in any executed instrument reviewed.

chapters.heading: What we know, and what we don’t

council_switch.explainer: Pressing this dims everything the council-facing summary did not describe. Some underlying instruments were incorporated by reference: the resolution authorised execution of “the Short Form Agreement and Addendum on file with the City Clerk.”

hard_cut.line: The records reviewed do not establish when each sharing relationship was configured.

lanes.label: What the City retains
lanes.body: The City stated it does not generate or keep copies of ALPR database search logs. It treats audit material as confidential intelligence data under Iowa Code §692.8.

lanes.label: What the City produced
lanes.body: One internal audit entry, dated 1 October 2025, reviewing 500 records. Department policy requiring regular audits of ALPR inquiries, issued 8 March 2024.

lanes.label: What the contract allows
lanes.body: Opt-in outbound sharing by setting, with no memorandum, notice, review or approval required. Chained sub-processor consent. Storage location in the vendor’s sole discretion. One audit right, running vendor to City.

lanes.label: What any actual transfer is established to show
lanes.body: Nothing. No transfer, query, hit or viewing record appears in anything produced. This is a statement about the record produced, not a statement that no such record exists anywhere.

known.text: The council approved $1,500,080 for M500 in-car video systems and Video Manager, on a consent agenda, on 20 November 2023.
Neither the resolution nor the council communication mentions plate reading, and both describe in-car video and video evidence management software.
The plate-reader sharing clause is in the executed Mobile Video Addendum, at page 9 of the 25-page clerk’s file.
$67,580 of plate-reader licensing and support was priced in an ordering document that is not in that file, and every delivered system carried an “M500 ALPR DVR” component.

A separate, earlier procurement — different vendor, different cooperative, different city agreement — bought the platform, three years of commercial national vehicle-location data and fixed cameras between July and September 2023, by administrative signature.
Plate readers entered the cooperative price list in September 2021 by a vendor change form stating they had been “mistakenly left off.” The underlying solicitation contains no plate-reader terms.
As of 17 August 2026 the City’s platform was configured to share detections with at least 155 agencies in 36 states and the District of Columbia, and to receive from 120 of them.
The only audit right in the executed agreements runs from the vendor to the City, and the City stated it does not keep copies of search logs.

unknown.text: When any of the 155 sharing relationships was configured. 151 of 155 rows carry no usable date, and no other record dates them.
Whether any plate record has ever been transferred to, queried by or viewed by any listed agency. No such record exists in anything produced.
Whether the addenda were physically before council members on 20 November 2023, or were placed in the clerk’s file at execution the same day.
What any individual council member read, knew, understood or intended. Item 32 was a consent item; this is outside the record and outside this exhibit.
How 130 purchased, 126 subscribed, 120 reported operational and 140 Mobile system records reconcile. No document reconciles them.
What “Customer Data” meant in November 2023. The definitional chain runs out of the produced record into a vendor-hosted addendum that may change from time to time.
What the “(F)” name prefix on 51 rows means, or what the “Inactive” prefix on five rows means. Neither is defined in any located documentation.
What fund the account code on the fixed-camera purchase order refers to. No document maps it. This is an open question, not a finding.

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — the 2026 renewal
sidebars.body: In June 2026 a council communication for continuing plate-reader software under a different cooperative contract printed “PREVIOUS COUNCIL ACTION(S): NONE.” It is a 2026 document and is never spliced into the 2023 chronology.

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — how the systems were counted
sidebars.body: The August 2026 systems export contains 149 top-level system rows — 140 Mobile, 7 IP, 2 Fixed — with 560 camera rows nested beneath them. Counting the seven IP lane units as cameras rather than systems gives the alternative shorthand of 142 systems and 567 cameras. Either convention is defensible. This exhibit uses the first and says so. One Mobile row is literally named “Unit number.”

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — four unit counts
sidebars.body: 130 purchased and licensed. 126 subscribed. 120 reported operational. 140 Mobile system records in the 2026 export. Four numbers, four sources, no reconciling document. This exhibit publishes all four and offers no explanation.

network_page.title: Explore the configuration
network_page.dek: Every relationship in the City of Des Moines’ August 2026 VehicleManager sharing export, as the reader chooses to see it. These are settings, not movements.
network_page.standing_note: Nothing on this page is animated to suggest motion. Counterparties are drawn as open rings, never as filled location dots. No connector is drawn by default. Select a ring to show that one relationship; select a state’s label to filter to that state. When you select an agency, one connector appears at once, without direction and without motion, labelled “configured to share.”
network_page.empty_state: No agency selected. 155 configured relationships, no connectors drawn.
network_page.table_caption: All 155 rows of the August 2026 sharing export, verbatim. This table is the accessible equivalent of the tile grid above and works without JavaScript.

records_page.title: The record
records_page.dek: Every instrument, chain, price, date, record layer and receipt behind this exhibit — as a chronology, as two contract chains, as the clerk’s document stack, and as a parts list.
records_page.corrections_note: This exhibit is built on a complete-record adjudication dated 3 September 2026, which corrected several figures and framings used in earlier RDP working notes. Those corrections are listed here so that the older versions are not reintroduced.

corrections.now: 36 states and the District of Columbia
corrections.why: The export’s State column holds 37 distinct values, one of which is the District of Columbia.

corrections.now: 149 top-level system rows (140 Mobile, 7 IP, 2 Fixed) with 560 nested cameras
corrections.why: The earlier shorthand counted the seven IP lane units as cameras. Both conventions are defensible; the exhibit states which it uses.

corrections.was: “Council saw the cameras but not the network.”
corrections.now: What the council-facing summary described, versus what the instruments contained, versus what the City had already contracted administratively
corrections.why: Item 32 was a consent item and the resolution incorporated the addendum by reference. Nothing in the record establishes what any member saw, read or knew.

corrections.now: Five change forms identified for contract 010720 in 2021
corrections.why: The 3 September 2021 form created the price list that the 14 September form says the plate reader was left off of.

corrections.was: “Customer Data is defined in the MCA.”
corrections.now: The customer agreement refers onward to a vendor-hosted Data Processing Addendum for that definition
corrections.why: The addendum is at a vendor URL, may be updated from time to time, and states that it prevails in a conflict.

corrections.now: The City stated it does not generate or keep copies of search logs
corrections.why: Department policy requires regular audits and one audit entry reviewing 500 records is in the record. Retention by the City is not the same as existence anywhere.

corrections.now: Two separately dated facts: contractual permission in 2023, observed configuration in 2026
corrections.why: 151 of 155 rows carry no date. No record establishes that chronology.
